questions.question: What model uses the same retrieved document to predict each target token across the complete sequence?
questions.supporting_excerpt: In one approach, RAG-Sequence, the model uses the same document to predict each target token.

questions.question: How does RAG-Token differ from RAG-Sequence in terms of latent document selection?
questions.answer: RAG-Token can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize accordingly, whereas RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document for the complete sequence.
questions.supporting_excerpt: In the RAG-Token model we can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize accordingly. This allows the generator to choose content from several documents when producing an answer.

questions.question: Under what condition are RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token equivalent?
questions.answer: They are equivalent for sequence classification tasks by considering the target class as a target sequence of length one.
questions.supporting_excerpt: Finally, we note that RAG can be used for sequence classiﬁcation tasks by considering the target class as a target sequence of length one, in which case RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent.

questions.question: What architecture does the DPR retriever component follow in RAG?
questions.supporting_excerpt: The retrieval component pη(z|x) is based on DPR [26]. DPR follows a bi-encoder architecture: pη(z|x) ∝exp d(z)⊤q(x)

questions.question: What specific model is used for the generator component in RAG, and how many parameters does it have?
questions.supporting_excerpt: We use BART-large [32], a pre-trained seq2seq transformer [58] with 400M parameters.

questions.question: How is the input x combined with the retrieved content z when generating text using BART in RAG?
questions.supporting_excerpt: To combine the input x with the retrieved content z when generating from BART, we simply concatenate them.

questions.question: In RAG, what term is used to refer to the document index versus the BART generator parameters θ?
questions.answer: The document index is referred to as non-parametric memory, and the BART generator parameters θ are referred to as parametric memory.
questions.supporting_excerpt: We refer to the document index as the non-parametric memory. 2.3 Generator: BART ... We refer to the BART generator parameters θ as the parametric memory henceforth.

questions.question: How many identical layers make up the Transformer encoder stack?
questions.supporting_excerpt: Encoder: The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers.

questions.question: What are the two sub-layers present in each layer of the Transformer encoder?
questions.answer: A multi-head self-attention mechanism and a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network.
questions.supporting_excerpt: Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position- wise fully connected feed-forward network.

questions.question: What is the output dimension (dmodel) of all sub-layers and embedding layers in the Transformer?
questions.supporting_excerpt: To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension dmodel = 512.

questions.question: What is the third sub-layer inserted into each layer of the Transformer decoder stack?
questions.answer: A sub-layer that performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack.
questions.supporting_excerpt: In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack.

questions.question: Why is the self-attention sub-layer modified in the Transformer decoder stack?
questions.answer: To prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions.
questions.supporting_excerpt: We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions.

questions.answer: Algorithm termination, resulting in an algorithm output.

questions.question: What is the lower bound on the running time of any comparison sort algorithm?
questions.supporting_excerpt: Height ≥dlg(n + 1)e − 1 = Ω(log n), so running time of any comparison sort is Ω(log n)

questions.question: What is the primary drawback of using a direct access array when the number of items n is much smaller than the universe of keys u (n ≪ u)?
questions.answer: It requires O(u) space, which is really bad if n ≪ u.
questions.supporting_excerpt: But space O(u), so really bad if n ≪ u... :(

questions.question: Why is no hash function injective when m ≪ u?
questions.supporting_excerpt: If m ≪ u, no hash function is injective by pigeonhole principle

questions.question: What are the two strategies mentioned for handling collisions where h(a) = h(b)?
questions.answer: Storing somewhere else in the array (open addressing) or storing in another data structure supporting dynamic set interface (chaining).
questions.supporting_excerpt: Can’t store both items at same index, so where to store? Either: – store somewhere else in the array (open addressing) ∗ complicated analysis, but common and practical – store in another data structure supporting dynamic set interface (chaining)

questions.question: In hashing with chaining, what is the chain size if keys are roughly evenly distributed over m indices where m = Ω(n)?
questions.supporting_excerpt: If keys roughly evenly distributed over indices, chain size is n/m = n/Ω(n) = O(1)!

questions.question: What mathematical formula represents the division hash function?
questions.supporting_excerpt: Hash Functions Division (bad): h(k) = (k mod m)
